title: Beyond Coercion: Thinking Deeper than Carrots and Sticks
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Prompted by what the COVID-19 school closures of spring 2020 revealed about student motivation, Stuart observes that many students are driven primarily by carrots and sticks — grades, credit, GPA — and argues this is not a character flaw in students but a byproduct of systems and the messages adults send about school's purpose. He contends that when educators are fuzzy about "what education is for," students rationally conclude that school is a purposeless thing to get through, producing a dehumanizing "play the game" mentality he compares to treating people like donkeys motivated only by carrots and sticks. Rather than abandoning a broad, knowledge-rich curriculum in favor of chasing relevance, he calls for educators to be able to clearly articulate education's purpose and to create classroom conditions for genuine, non-coerced motivation. He grounds this in his five-key-beliefs framework (credibility, value, belonging, effort, efficacy), arguing it humanizes students, empowers teachers, and gives schools a shared goal, and closes by noting the shift doesn't require dismantling existing grading systems, just building humanizing practices alongside them.
points: Stuart reframes the "play the game" motivation problem exposed by COVID remote learning as a systems-and-messaging failure, not a defect in students themselves.

He cites researcher Sarah Malin's finding that only about a quarter of high schoolers have identified and are pursuing a life purpose, framing carrots-and-sticks motivation as a symptom of purpose-starved schooling.

His proposed fix is deliberately non-disruptive: keep a broad, knowledge-rich curriculum, but ensure every educator can articulate what education is for and can create conditions for non-coerced motivation.

The five key beliefs (credibility, value, belonging, effort, efficacy) are positioned as the practical framework that humanizes students, empowers teachers, and gives schools a shared, malleable goal.
quotes: This "play the game" mentality is not something to blame on the children. Instead, it is a fruit of our systems and a fruit of the kinds of things we say to students about learning, school, and what it's all for.

Again and again, we come back to a central principle here on the blog: when the adults in a student's life are fuzzy on the purpose of an education — on Everest, as we say — then all types of problems result.
The more I observe the effects of this "play the game" mentality, the more I see that it is deeply dehumanizing. I mean this literally. Carrots and sticks are for donkeys, not people.

Sarah Malin, a former colleague of Bill Damon at the Stanford Center on Adolescence and author of Teaching for Purpose, found in interviewing hundreds of adolescent students that only a quarter of high schoolers (and fewer in younger grades) had identified and were pursuing a purpose for their lives.
My point is not that we ought to sideline a broad, knowledge-rich, sequential curriculum for one focused on relevance or on helping students find their purposes.

In short, carrots and sticks don't have to be the primary thing driving our children to do the work of learning, and we don't even need to remove the carrots/sticks system in order to start enacting this humanizing change in our classrooms and schools.
